title: DACA Recipients Face Mounting Deportation Threats as Government Dismantles Protections
excerpt: At least 85 DACA recipients have been deported since Trump took office, while renewal delays leave hundreds of thousands in legal limbo.
body:
• At least 85 DACA recipients have been deported since Trump's second term began, with the Board of Immigration Appeals ruling that DACA status alone is insufficient to halt removal proceedings.
  • DACA renewal processing times have stretched from weeks to six months or more, leaving recipients without work authorization and accruing unlawful presence.
  • Tucson resident Karla Toledo, a DACA recipient for over a decade, was detained without a warrant and placed into deportation proceedings twice within 24 hours.
  • Roughly 506,000 DACA recipients nationwide face heightened enforcement risk under a February 2025 policy memo that ended exemptions for noncitizens with approved immigration benefits.

When Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived at Karla Toledo's Tucson home in May without a warrant, they targeted a woman who had lived in Arizona for 30 years. Brought to the U.S. as a toddler, Toledo had spent more than a decade under DACA protection — the kind of legal shield that, until recently, kept people like her safe from deportation.

Her case was dismissed by an immigration judge on June 2 at the government's own request. Less than 24 hours later, DHS filed a new notice to appear, restarting deportation proceedings — this time jointly with her husband. Her attorney, Mo Goldman, accused the government of retaliation.

"They couldn't even copy and paste the first notice to appear correctly. On the second notice, they misspelled her middle name."

— Mo Goldman, Immigration Attorney

A Legal Shield Under Siege

Toledo's case is part of a broader pattern. In April 2026, the Board of Immigration Appeals issued a precedent-setting decision in the case of Catalina "Xóchitl" Santiago-Santiago, ruling that DACA status is not sufficient reason to terminate deportation proceedings. The ruling effectively stripped what had been a de facto shield for recipients across the country.

That decision followed a February 2025 policy memo directing USCIS employees to no longer exempt any noncitizens from potential removal proceedings, including those with approved immigration benefits like DACA. By June 2025, USCIS reported initiating removal proceedings against more than 26,700 people under the new policy.

U.S. Congressman Joaquin Castro announced this summer that at least 85 DACA recipients have been deported since Trump took office again — a number attorneys say is likely an undercount.

Renewal Delays Compound the Crisis

Beyond deportation, DACA recipients face another threat: bureaucratic slowdowns. Renewal processing times have ballooned from what once took weeks to an average of more than three months, according to USCIS's own data. Attorneys and recipients report real-world waits of six months or more.

The consequences are cascading. When DACA lapses before renewal, recipients lose work authorization and, in many states, their driver's licenses. Time spent in the U.S. after a lapse can be counted as "unlawful presence," potentially barring future legal pathways.

"My constituent services team currently has over 100 open cases related to DACA renewals," said U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva in a statement. "We are seeing significantly longer processing times than in previous years, with some cases pending since last November."

"They are intentionally dragging their feet on DACA renewals, trying to create a class of individuals where they have to work under the table."

— Mo Goldman, Toledo's Attorney

The Legal Landscape

The legal underpinnings of DACA remain fragile. In January 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit found DACA's grant of work authorization unlawful while suggesting its deportation protections could be separated from work permits. In September 2025, the federal government submitted a proposal to Judge Hanen that would tie DACA benefits to a recipient's address — meaning simply moving to Texas could trigger revocation of both work authorization and lawful presence within 15 days.

A ruling on that proposal could come at any time.

The American Immigration Council estimates roughly 506,000 individuals hold active DACA status, with nearly 28% — more than 141,000 — residing in California. An estimated 6,784 educators across California's K-12 and higher education systems hold DACA status.

What Comes Next

For Toledo, the fight continues. Her DACA status was set to expire in July, with her renewal application — submitted in January — still pending months later. Goldman said he is working to sever her case from her husband's, arguing that her DACA status should shield her from removal.

Tucson Mayor Regina Romero framed the issue as a test of broader values. "DACA recipients came forward, registered with the federal government, underwent background checks and followed the rules," Romero said. "They should not be punished for doing so."

Immigration attorneys warn that the government's approach represents a fundamental shift — from a system that rewarded compliance to one that punishes it. For the half-million DACA recipients who came forward, registered, and played by the rules, the question now is whether those rules still mean anything.
nri_angle: DACA recipients include thousands of Indian-origin immigrants who arrived as children; the dismantling of protections affects South Asian dreamers navigating the U.S. immigration system.
author: Diaspora Desk
